title: Setting up
status: DRAFT for Ilan's review (20 Nov 2026). Not filmed. Recording brief: RECORDING.md. Real data entry only: each setting-up step is done on the website in the sample company and filmed step by step (kind "steps").
source: docs/learning/film/SERIES_PLAN.md section 5 (episode 2's objective); the starter kit's drawing set (A-201, A-301), materials and suppliers workbook, Periyar's rate card and the building permit (apps/dashboard/public/learn/kit, kit.json's catches); the sample company's setup pages as they stand after the guided project's chapters 2 and 3, 20 Nov 2026. Construction practice: typical, to be checked by someone who has run sites.
objective: By the end you can list what must exist before day 1 and who sets it up: the company, the project and its sites, the team on WhatsApp, drawings and documents, items, suppliers and rates, the schedule and the material plan, and the daily report time.

scenes.title: Setting up
beats: The second of November, six in the morning. Ravi, the site engineer, is at Green Villa with ten workers and a lorry of sand.
In an hour he will send his first message. Attendance, the sand that came, the work begun.
Where does that message go? Who reads it? What is it measured against? All of that is decided in the two weeks before. This episode is those two weeks.

lines.text: Everything a message needs, ready before it is sent

scenes.title: Set up before day 1, or chase it for nine months
beats: Every builder sets up a job. The only question is when.
Set up before day one, and every message from site lands in the right place: the right site, the right BOQ line, the right supplier.
Set up later, and the first weeks pile up. Deliveries with no supplier, work with no line, stock nobody counted, and a report nobody gets.
Two weeks of setting up save months of sorting out.

scenes.title: What must exist before the first message
beats: Here is everything that must exist before Ravi's first message.
The company, with its name and letterhead. The project, its two sites, the Main block and the Annex, and the time its daily report goes out.
The team, each person with a role and a WhatsApp number. Without a number, a person cannot report from site.
The drawings, checked, and every document in one place: the permit, the contract, the estimate.
What the site will use and who supplies it: the items, the suppliers, their rates, and what is already on site.
And the plan: when each part of the work happens, and the material it needs, week by week.

scenes.title: Who sets up what
beats: Who sets up what?
Ramesh, the owner, sets up the company, the project and its sites, and the team.
Anil, the project manager, checks the drawings, plans the work, and fills in the items, suppliers and rates.
Meera, in accounts, puts in what the company already owes, and where its money is kept.
And Ravi gets one thing: his number added, so that on day one he can simply start talking.

scenes.title: The roof, as the elevation draws it
beats: Anil starts with the drawings from episode one. This time he reads the sheets against each other, because a mistake often hides between two of them.
This is A-201, the front elevation: the house seen from the road.
The roof slab is marked here: six hundred and sixty centimetres above the ground.

paper.pdf: Green Villa - drawing set rev A.pdf

scenes.eyebrow: The paper · Drawing A-301, the section
scenes.title: The same roof, five centimetres lower
beats: And this is A-301, the section: the house cut through, so you see every floor's height.
The same roof: six hundred and fifty-five.
Five centimetres. Nobody would notice on paper. On site, it decides where the carpenters set the shuttering, the day the roof is poured.
Found now, it is one phone call to the architect. Found after the pour, it is a broken slab, or a staircase that does not fit.

scenes.title: The drawings, read before they are built
beats: In Mesiri, Anil drops the whole drawing set on Drawing check.
It reads every sheet in a moment: eight sheets, four floors, six levels, the rooms and their sizes.
And it says what does not agree. The roof: plus six sixty on the elevation, plus six fifty-five on the section. The same level, drawn two ways?
The toilet upstairs is drawn smaller than the one below it, though toilets stack. Intended? And episode one's copied bedroom label is here too.
Two things to ask the architect, and one to check, before a single brick.

scenes.eyebrow: In Mesiri · Documents, Live plans, Places
scenes.title: Kept, and turned into places
beats: Next, Anil keeps the set in Documents. Mesiri reads its title block and files it under Drawings: A-101, revision A.
With it, the building permit from the municipality, under approvals and permits. When a drawing is revised, the new one goes in as revision B, and everyone opens the latest.
The same drawings become a live plan. One tap, Track on site, and the fourteen footings and every room on the drawings become places the site can report on.
Places now lists two floors and twenty rooms, from the plans, typed by nobody. Later, when Ravi says plastering done in bedroom two, it lands on that room.

scenes.title: What the office already knows, in one Excel
beats: Next, what the site will use, and who supplies it. Anil has it in one Excel, the way most offices do.
Four sheets: the items, the suppliers, the stock already on site, and the least each site should hold.
One line matters to Meera: the company already owes Colour World Paints twelve thousand five hundred rupees, from before. If it is not put in now, it is forgotten, or paid twice.
And the least to hold: a hundred bags of cement at the Main block, forty at the Annex. Below that, someone must order.

scenes.title: The Excel goes in as it is
beats: In Mesiri, Bring your data takes things in the order a job needs them: the projects and sites, the team, the materials and suppliers, the BOQ, the drawings.
The workbook goes in as it is. Mesiri shows what it read before anything is saved: twelve rows. The cement, Malabar and Joy Tiling are already in, so it leaves them alone. Then Import.
And anything else? Send the file on WhatsApp, with a line saying what it is.

scenes.title: The price agreed, in writing
beats: Then the rates. Periyar Sand and Aggregates sends its rate card: M sand at one thousand six hundred and fifty rupees a cubic metre, delivered at site.
Before GST, and any change told in writing, a week before.
Put the agreed rates in now, and every delivery is checked against them. In a few weeks, Periyar's sand will start coming at seventeen fifty. Mesiri will show it the day it happens.

scenes.title: When each part of the work happens
beats: Now the plan. The schedule already has its sections, straight from the BOQ: earthwork, concrete, masonry, plastering, all nine. And its finish, from the contract: the thirty-first of July.
What it needs is dates. Quick plan puts the sections one after another from the start day. Anil sets the days each will take, so the last one ends by the handover: about two hundred and seventy days.
Saved, and late means something at once. In the sample company the earthwork is already behind this plan, and Mesiri says what that does: the handover moves fifty-four days.

scenes.title: What to buy, and when
beats: With the dates and the BOQ together, Mesiri works out the material plan: what each week's work needs, against what is in stock and on order.
For Green Villa's cement: about ninety-six bags a week once the concrete starts, against a hundred and twenty-two in stock. So it says when to order: four hundred bags, by the second of December.
But only six of the thirty-four lines say what they use. The plan is honest about it: fill in the rest, and it covers the whole job.
A week turns red before it runs short, not on the day the site stops.

scenes.title: Everyone, with a role and a number
beats: Last, the people. Ramesh adds the team: Anil, Meera and Ravi, each with a role, and the projects they work on.
The role decides what each one sees. Ravi sees his sites' day, but never the rupees. Meera sees the bills and the payments.

And the number decides who can talk to Mesiri. Look: no one here has a WhatsApp number yet, and Mesiri says so. Ramesh opens Ravi's menu and types his number. Until it is in, Ravi's first message on day one goes nowhere.
And each project's report. Green Villa's day closes at six, and the report goes by nine. Ramesh switches on send automatically, and adds Doctor Krishnan, who agreed to get it on WhatsApp.

scenes.title: Five ways a job starts badly
beats: Five ways a job starts badly.
A number missing: the site's messages go nowhere, and the office finds out a week later.
Drawings not checked: the roof level is argued about on the day of the pour.
No least-stock: the cement runs out on a Friday, and the masons go home.
An old balance not put in: a supplier is paid twice, or argues for a year. And no dates: nobody can say whether the job is late.

footer.text: Each one costs minutes now, and weeks later.

scenes.title: Three questions
beats: Three questions. Pause, and answer them before you go on.
One: what must Ravi have before he can report from site? A WhatsApp number, on the team, with his role and his sites.
Two: the elevation says plus six sixty, the section says plus six fifty-five. What do you do, and when? Ask the architect, before the roof is shuttered.
Three: why put in what the company already owes? So nobody pays it twice, and the supplier's account starts right.
Next: a day on site. One Monday at the Annex, seven months in: from Ravi's first message to the report at nine.
